newsitem.title: UK: Shell announces shortlist for Brent Spar disposal.
newsitem.headline: Shell announces shortlist for Brent Spar disposal.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell Group on Monday said six contractors have been selected to develop possible alternative solutions for disposal of the giant Brent Spar North oil storage and loading buoy.
The six companies have been asked to make detailed proposals for 11 different ideas for re-using Brent Spar's component parts or scrapping it onshore.
Shell said the contractors have until the end of April before making commercial bids for alternatives to the deep sea disposal approved by the UK government almost two years ago.

"The proposals now to be developed represent the best of those we were offered, while also maintaining a good range of potential solutions," said Eric Faulds, Decommissioning Manager for Shell UK Exploration and Production (Shell Expro), which operates in the North Sea on behalf of Shell and Exxon.
Shell in the summer of 1995 was forced to abandon its plans to ditch Brent Spar in the Atlantic in the face of a high-profile campaign by environmental group Greenpeace.

Companies asked to develop solutions for Brent Spar are as follows: U.S. Halliburton Co British unit Brown and Root Energy Services; Kvaerner Stolt Seaway Alliance (KSSA) of Norway; a joint venture between Britain's Alfred McAlpine and Doris of France; a joint venture between Thyssen Stahluion GMBH of Germany and Norway's Aker NC; a joint venture between Britain's John D.Wood and Norway's GMC; Britain's AMEC Process and Energy.
Brown and Root, KSSA and Thyssen/Aker all proposed methods of onshore disposal, at yards in Britain or Norway.
McAlpine/Doris and KSSA suggested using the Spar for quay extension projects.
AMEC proposed using sections of the rig in a coastal defence scheme planned off the east coast of England.
KSSA and Wood-GMC identified potential clients with an interest in using the Spar topside for offshore training facilities in Norway.
KSSA also submitted late proposals for conversion into a a floating dry dock gate and for a fish farm development.

Shell must convince the British government that any alternative solution -- balancing safety, technical feasibility, economics, environmental impact and public acceptability -- is superior to deep sea disposal.

"The focus of our effort is to find a solution which is at least as good or better than deep sea disposal," said Shell Expro Managing Director Heinz Rothermund. "This remains the benchmark for comparison before we again make a recommendation to the government for approval."
Rothermund said independent specialists would be asked to review the detailed proposals and a final recommendation for the British government should be ready by the end of this year.
Decommissioning could get underway by the spring of 1998.
"This is an exciting competition and still wide open," said Decommissioning Manager Eric Faulds. "We genuinely do not know what the eventual solution will be."
Faulds said the cost of preparing the 11 proposals would be in the region of 1-1.5 million stg.
Faulds estimate Shell would have spent almost 20 million stg on Spar's disposal even before awarding a final contract.
The company has been paying 20,000 stg a month in rent to keep the 14,500 tonne rig parked in a Norwegian fjord.
It had already spent 10 million stg on the obselete rig's disposal before a public outcry forced it to back down on the original plans for dumping at sea.
--Richard Mably, London newsroom +44 171 542 8060
